questions.stem: A 62 year old woman sees her GP with 6 months of morning headaches and difficulty concentrating at work. Her husband now sleeps in the spare room because of her loud snoring and says she sometimes stops breathing, then snorts awake. Her BMI is 34 kg/m² and neck circumference 42 cm. Her BP is 152/94 mmHg. Thyroid function tests and fundoscopy are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas, morning headaches, poor concentration and hypertension in an obese patient is OSA.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Partner-reported snoring and apnoeas plus morning headaches in an obese woman.

elim: Low mood and anhedonia would lead; it does not cause witnessed apnoeas.
Thyroid function tests are normal.
Headaches with papilloedema; fundoscopy is normal and it does not cause apnoeas.
Sudden sleep attacks and cataplexy in a young person, not loud snoring with apnoeas.

steps.x: E: Obstructive sleep apnoea. Snoring + witnessed apnoeas + daytime symptoms in an obese patient = OSA.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is referred to the sleep clinic because his wife has seen him stop breathing during sleep. He has ischaemic heart disease and a BMI of 31 kg/m². He feels tired during the day. The sleep physician wants to decide whether the history points to obstructive or to central sleep apnoea before the study.
questions.q: Which feature of the history would most support obstructive sleep apnoea?
o: Breathing pauses witnessed by his wife
questions.e: Loud snoring reflects a narrowed, collapsing upper airway; central sleep apnoea causes pauses without loud snoring.

steps.x: The question asks: Which feature of the history would most support obstructive sleep apnoea?

clues: obstructive or to central sleep apnoea
steps.x: You need the feature that separates an obstructed airway from loss of drive.

elim: Seen in both obstructive and central sleep apnoea.
Occurs in both because both fragment sleep.
Opioids suppress ventilatory drive and point to central sleep apnoea.
Typical of central sleep apnoea too; does not separate them.

steps.x: D: Loud snoring between pauses. Central apnoea = pauses WITHOUT loud snoring; snoring means obstruction.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has loud snoring and his partner has seen him stop breathing at night. He feels unrefreshed and falls asleep in meetings. He drinks 4 units of alcohol a week and takes no medication. His BMI is 23 kg/m². Examination shows a small, receded jaw and very large tonsils that almost meet in the midline.
questions.q: Which is the most likely contributing factor to his condition?
o: Anatomical narrowing of the upper airway
questions.e: In a slim patient, large tonsils and retrognathia narrow the pharynx and cause OSA.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely contributing factor to his condition?
Classic OSA symptoms but not obese; the examination shows structural narrowing.

elim: That is central sleep apnoea, which lacks loud snoring.
His BMI is normal.
No features given; the examination shows a structural cause.
He takes no medication and drinks little.

steps.x: A: Anatomical narrowing of the upper airway. Not every OSA patient is obese: anatomical obstruction is a risk factor.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has had worsening snoring for 2 weeks. His partner says it has become much louder, with long pauses in his breathing followed by gasps, and he is now very sleepy at work. Two weeks ago he started a new tablet for back muscle spasm. His BMI is 29 kg/m². He also takes amlodipine, omeprazole and paracetamol.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to have worsened his condition?
questions.e: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam (used for muscle spasm) relax the pharyngeal dilators and worsen OSA, as alcohol does.

steps.x: The question asks: Which drug is most likely to have worsened his condition?

clues: Two weeks ago he started a new tablet for back muscle spasm
steps.x: Snoring and apnoeas worsened after a new muscle relaxant.

elim: Long-standing and does not relax pharyngeal muscles.
An NSAID; it does not reduce airway muscle tone.
Long-standing; no effect on the airway.
Long-standing; no sedative effect.

steps.x: B: Diazepam. Sedatives and alcohol worsen OSA by reducing pharyngeal muscle tone.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness for many years but has refused a sleep study. He has hypertension treated with three drugs. His BMI is 38 kg/m². His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 158/96 mmHg. He asks what the long-term risks of leaving his condition untreated are.
questions.q: Which is the most likely long-term complication of his untreated condition?
questions.e: Untreated OSA increases cardiovascular disease: hypertension, heart failure and stroke.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely long-term complication of his untreated condition?
Untreated OSA with resistant hypertension.

elim: A suppurative airway disease; not caused by OSA.
Can mimic OSA but is not a complication of it.
An interstitial disease unrelated to upper airway collapse.
Autoimmune; not caused by OSA.

steps.x: D: Stroke. OSA complications are cardiovascular (hypertension, heart failure, stroke) and accidents.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man who drives a delivery van has polysomnography confirming severe obstructive sleep apnoea. His Epworth Sleepiness Score is 18. He says he struggles to stay awake on long afternoon routes. He has no chest pain or breathlessness. His BMI is 35 kg/m², pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 142/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most immediate danger from his condition?
questions.e: Excessive daytime sleepiness makes road accidents the most immediate risk; he must stop driving and notify the DVLA.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most immediate danger from his condition?
A professional driver with severe sleepiness.

elim: Not expected; his problem is sleepiness, not ventilatory failure.
A long-term cardiovascular risk, not the immediate danger here.
Not a direct consequence of OSA.
Rare; the clear immediate risk is a road accident.

steps.x: B: Falling asleep while driving. Sleepiness from OSA causes accidents: always ask about driving.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and a BMI of 36 kg/m² has overnight polysomnography. His Epworth Sleepiness Score is 14. He is expected to have obstructive sleep apnoea. The sleep technician explains that the study records nasal airflow, chest and abdominal movement, and oxygen saturation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on polysomnography?
o: Absent airflow with absent respiratory effort
Absent airflow with continued chest and abdominal effort
questions.e: In OSA the airway collapses so airflow stops while the chest and abdomen keep trying to breathe.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on polysomnography?
Expected OSA; the study measures both airflow and effort.

elim: Loss of drive with no effort is central sleep apnoea.
Crescendo-decrescendo breathing is a central pattern seen in heart failure.
Apnoeas cause intermittent desaturation.
Suggests obesity hypoventilation, not repeated collapse.

steps.x: B: Absent airflow with continued chest and abdominal effort. Obstructive = no airflow but effort continues; central = no airflow and no effort.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has been sent by his partner because of loud snoring and pauses in his breathing at night. His collar size is 19 inches (48 cm) and his BMI is 37 kg/m². He drinks 3 pints of beer most evenings. He has no breathlessness. His BP is 148/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which other symptom is he most likely to report?
o: Early morning waking with low mood
questions.e: Nocturnal hypercapnia in OSA causes morning headaches, along with daytime sleepiness and poor concentration.

steps.x: The question asks: Which other symptom is he most likely to report?

clues: loud snoring and pauses in his breathing
steps.x: A classic OSA picture with large neck, obesity and alcohol.

elim: A feature of narcolepsy, not OSA.
Suggests depression.
A feature of heart failure; he has no breathlessness.
Restless legs syndrome, a separate sleep disorder.

steps.x: C: Morning headaches. OSA: snoring, apnoeas, morning headache, daytime sleepiness, poor concentration.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a raised haemoglobin on a blood test arranged for tiredness. He has never smoked and has no lung disease. His wife reports very loud snoring and gasping at night. His BMI is 39 kg/m². His oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air while awake. There is no splenomegaly and JAK2 mutation testing is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Nocturnal hypoxia in OSA drives renal erythropoietin release and a secondary polycythaemia, with normal awake saturations.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

clues: very loud snoring and gasping at night
steps.x: Isolated raised red cells in an obese snorer with normal awake oxygen.

elim: He has never smoked and has no lung disease.
Raises haematocrit relatively but does not explain the snoring and gasping.
JAK2 is negative and there is no splenomegaly, and the white cells and platelets are normal.
A rare cause of polycythaemia with no supporting features here.

steps.x: C: Obstructive sleep apnoea. Secondary polycythaemia with normal daytime saturations: think OSA.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with long-standing untreated obstructive sleep apnoea has 3 months of ankle swelling and breathlessness on exertion. His JVP is raised, there is a loud second heart sound in the pulmonary area and pitting oedema to the knees. His lungs are clear. Echocardiography shows a raised pulmonary artery pressure with normal left ventricular function.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?
o: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction from nocturnal hypoxia
questions.e: Recurrent nocturnal hypoxia causes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?

clues: loud second heart sound in the pulmonary area
steps.x: Right heart failure with pulmonary hypertension in untreated OSA.

elim: Would not cause a raised pulmonary artery pressure or loud P2.
Left ventricular function is normal and the lungs are clear.
No murmur is described and the left heart is normal.
Causes oedema but not a raised JVP or pulmonary hypertension.

steps.x: B: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction from nocturnal hypoxia. OSA can cause pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale through hypoxic vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with type 2 diabetes has 1 year of tiredness. He falls asleep in the afternoon and his wife has left the bedroom because of his snoring and breath-holding. His BMI is 41 kg/m². His oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air. HbA1c is 52 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Snoring with breath-holding and daytime sleepiness in an obese man is OSA; normal awake PaCO2 excludes obesity hypoventilation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Witnessed apnoeas and sleepiness in severe obesity; awake gases normal.

elim: No smoking history or breathlessness, and gases are normal.
Thyroid function is normal.
Needs daytime hypercapnia; his awake PaCO2 is normal.
HbA1c 52 is reasonable control and does not cause apnoeas.

steps.x: D: Obstructive sleep apnoea. OSA has normal awake gases; obesity hypoventilation has daytime hypercapnia.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has repeated drops in oxygen saturation to 82% with loud snoring and pauses in breathing while asleep in recovery after a knee operation. Back on the ward he says he always feels tired and his wife complains about his snoring. His BMI is 33 kg/m². His Epworth Sleepiness Score is 13.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Overnight polysomnography is the gold-standard test that confirms OSA and its severity.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

clues: loud snoring and pauses in breathing while asleep
steps.x: Observed apnoeas and desaturation in sleep with daytime sleepiness.

elim: Shows daytime gas exchange; does not confirm apnoeas during sleep.
Not a diagnostic test for OSA.
Used for narcolepsy.
Tests airflow obstruction in the lower airways, not sleep apnoea.

steps.x: D: Polysomnography. Diagnosis of OSA = (nocturnal) polysomnography.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman tells her GP she nods off whenever she sits down to read and once fell asleep at a red light. Her partner says she snores. Her BMI is 31 kg/m² and BP 138/86 mmHg. The GP wants a validated questionnaire that grades how likely she is to doze in everyday situations.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate tool to use?
questions.e: The Epworth Sleepiness Score grades the chance of dozing in 8 everyday situations; STOP-BANG estimates OSA risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate tool to use?

clues: grades how likely she is to doze in everyday situations
steps.x: The tool must measure dozing likelihood.

elim: Grades conscious level in acute illness.
Grades breathlessness.
Screens for depression.
Estimates the risk of having OSA, not the degree of daytime sleepiness.

steps.x: A: Epworth Sleepiness Score. Sleepiness = Epworth; OSA risk = STOP-BANG.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with snoring and witnessed apnoeas completes an Epworth Sleepiness Score in clinic. He has a moderate chance of dozing while reading and watching TV and a high chance when lying down in the afternoon. His total score is 12. His BMI is 32 kg/m².

visual.title: Epworth Sleepiness Score
visual.label: Score 12
visual.caption: 11 to 12 is mild excessive daytime sleepiness.

questions.q: Which best describes his daytime sleepiness?
questions.e: An Epworth score of 11 to 12 is mild excessive daytime sleepiness.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes his daytime sleepiness?
Place 12 on the Epworth bands.

elim: That band is 0 to 5.
That band is 13 to 15.
That band is 6 to 10.
That band is 16 to 24.

steps.x: B: Mild excessive daytime sleepiness. Epworth: 0-5 low, 6-10 normal, 11-12 mild, 13-15 moderate, 16-24 severe.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has an Epworth Sleepiness Score of 8 at a sleep clinic review. She snores and her partner has seen occasional pauses in her breathing. She works as a teacher and drives to work. Her BMI is 30 kg/m² and BP 132/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which best describes her daytime sleepiness on this score?
questions.e: A score of 6 to 10 is normal daytime sleepiness; without excessive sleepiness OSA is not a driving risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes her daytime sleepiness on this score?
Place 8 on the Epworth bands.

elim: That band is 0 to 5.
That band is 11 to 12.
That band is 13 to 15.
That band is 16 to 24.

steps.x: D: Normal daytime sleepiness. 6 to 10 is normal: sleepiness, not snoring, drives DVLA decisions.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man attends a pre-assessment clinic before bariatric surgery. His BMI is 46 kg/m² and neck circumference 45 cm. He has treated hypertension and his wife says he snores. The nurse wants a quick screen to decide whether he needs referral for a sleep study before his anaesthetic.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: STOP-BANG (Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnoea, Pressure, BMI, Age, Neck, Gender) screens for OSA before referral for polysomnography.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
A screening tool is needed first.

elim: Does not screen for sleep apnoea.
Not a screening test for OSA.
The diagnostic test, done after screening suggests risk.
Tests lower airway obstruction, not OSA.

steps.x: E: STOP-BANG questionnaire. Screen with STOP-BANG, confirm with polysomnography.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with heart failure is reported by his wife to stop breathing for long periods at night. She says he does not snore. His BMI is 26 kg/m². His respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. The team needs to know whether the pauses are obstructive or central.
questions.q: Which investigation would best distinguish the two?
questions.e: Polysomnography records airflow and chest/abdominal effort, so it separates obstructive (effort present) from central (no effort) apnoeas.

steps.x: The question asks: Which investigation would best distinguish the two?
Need a test measuring respiratory effort during sleep.

elim: Daytime gases are usually normal in both.
Grades sleepiness; cannot tell obstructive from central.
Shows desaturation but not whether respiratory effort is present.
A screening score, not a test of effort during apnoeas.

steps.x: D: Polysomnography. Polysomnography is gold standard and measures effort, separating OSA from central apnoea.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has polysomnography confirming moderate obstructive sleep apnoea and has started CPAP. His BMI is 37 kg/m². He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week and goes to bed at the same time each night. He asks what he can do himself to improve his condition.
questions.q: Which is the most important lifestyle intervention?
questions.e: Weight loss is the most important lifestyle measure because pharyngeal fat drives airway collapse.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important lifestyle intervention?
Obese patient asking about self-help.

elim: Sleep hygiene only; much less effective than weight loss.
Does not treat airway collapse.
He already has a regular routine; it helps less than weight loss.
Good advice generally but not the key factor in OSA.

steps.x: E: Weight loss. Weight loss is the most important lifestyle change in OSA.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has polysomnography confirming severe obstructive sleep apnoea. Her Epworth Sleepiness Score is 17. She has begun a diet and exercise programme. She asks the respiratory consultant for an operation to stop her snoring because she has read about throat surgery online. She has no tonsillar enlargement.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: CPAP is first-line and gold standard for symptomatic OSA; surgery is a rarely used third-line option.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: asks the respiratory consultant for an operation
steps.x: Severe symptomatic OSA; surgery requested.

elim: Second-line for mild to moderate OSA when CPAP is not tolerated.
Does not treat airway collapse.
Upper airway surgery is third-line and rarely used.
A sedative that worsens OSA.

steps.x: A: Continuous positive airway pressure. CPAP first; MAD second; surgery third and rare.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has polysomnography showing mild obstructive sleep apnoea with an Epworth Sleepiness Score of 12. He tried CPAP for 2 months but removed the mask every night because he felt claustrophobic, despite trying different masks. He has lost 5 kg. His BMI is 29 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: A mandibular advancement device is second-line for mild to moderate OSA when CPAP cannot be tolerated.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Mild OSA and CPAP intolerance.

elim: Third-line and rarely used.
The problem is mask intolerance, not pressure.
Does not prevent airway collapse.
A sedative that worsens OSA.

steps.x: D: Mandibular advancement device. Mild to moderate OSA + CPAP intolerance = mandibular advancement device.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man with moderate obstructive sleep apnoea cannot tolerate CPAP despite mask refitting and humidification. A mandibular advancement device did not improve his symptoms after 6 months. Examination shows grossly enlarged tonsils. His BMI is 25 kg/m² and his Epworth Sleepiness Score remains 14.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Upper airway surgery is a rarely used third-line option, here justified by failure of CPAP and MAD with a clear anatomical cause.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: mandibular advancement device did not improve
steps.x: First and second line have failed and there is a structural cause.

elim: He cannot tolerate CPAP at all.
Does not treat the obstruction.
Masks sleepiness but leaves the airway untreated.
Far too drastic before targeted upper airway surgery.

steps.x: A: Elective upper airway surgery. Surgery is third-line: after CPAP and MAD, with anatomical obstruction.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man has polysomnography showing mild obstructive sleep apnoea. His Epworth Sleepiness Score is 7 and he has never felt sleepy while driving. He drives a car to work. He has started a weight loss programme. He asks whether he must stop driving or tell anyone about his diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about driving?
o: Continue driving without notifying the DVLA
Notify the DVLA and stop driving
Notify the DVLA only if he has an accident
questions.e: Mild OSA without excessive daytime sleepiness is not a driving risk and the DVLA need not be told.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice about driving?
Mild disease, normal Epworth.

elim: Only for moderate or severe OSA with excessive daytime sleepiness.
Wrong rule; notification depends on sleepiness and severity.
No such rule; mild OSA without sleepiness is not a driving risk.
Not required without excessive sleepiness.

steps.x: A: Continue driving without notifying the DVLA. DVLA only for moderate/severe OSA WITH excessive daytime sleepiness.

questions.stem: A 59 year old bus driver has polysomnography confirming moderate obstructive sleep apnoea. His Epworth Sleepiness Score is 15 and he admits to nodding off at traffic lights. He is about to start CPAP. He asks whether he can keep working while he waits for treatment to take effect.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about driving?
o: Continue driving and notify the DVLA once CPAP starts
Continue driving without notifying the DVLA
Notify the DVLA only if he has an accident
Stop driving and notify the DVLA
questions.e: Confirmed moderate OSA with excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth 15) requires him to stop driving and notify the DVLA.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice about driving?
Moderate OSA with moderate excessive sleepiness in a professional driver.

elim: He is sleepy now and must stop driving now.
Moderate OSA with excessive sleepiness must be notified.
Not a recognised restriction.
Wrong rule; notification depends on sleepiness and severity.

steps.x: E: Stop driving and notify the DVLA. Moderate/severe OSA + excessive sleepiness = stop driving, tell the DVLA.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with severe obstructive sleep apnoea has used CPAP every night for 3 months. Download data show good adherence and a low residual apnoea count, but he still feels sleepy on some mornings. He drinks 4 pints of lager each evening before bed. His BMI is 31 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Switch to a mandibular advancement device
questions.e: Evening alcohol relaxes the pharyngeal muscles and worsens OSA; reducing it is key lifestyle advice alongside CPAP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: 4 pints of lager each evening before bed
steps.x: CPAP works but heavy evening alcohol.

elim: Address the reversible cause first.
Third-line and he is adherent to effective CPAP.
A sedative that worsens OSA.
CPAP is working; MAD is less effective.

steps.x: B: Advise stopping evening alcohol. Lifestyle alongside CPAP: weight loss, less alcohol, good sleep hygiene.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with obstructive sleep apnoea asks why his breathing stops only when he is asleep, even though he can breathe normally through the same throat during the day. His BMI is 32 kg/m². Awake, his oxygen saturation is 97% and he has no stridor.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his apnoeas?
o: Intermittent loss of central ventilatory drive
Loss of pharyngeal dilator muscle tone during sleep
questions.e: During sleep pharyngeal dilator muscle tone falls, so a narrowed pharynx collapses repeatedly.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his apnoeas?
Collapse happens only when muscle tone falls in sleep.

elim: A lower airway mechanism (asthma), not upper airway collapse.
That is central sleep apnoea.
Would cause stridor awake too.
Effort continues during obstructive apnoeas.

steps.x: D: Loss of pharyngeal dilator muscle tone during sleep. OSA = sleep-related loss of pharyngeal dilator tone and airway collapse.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman develops loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas after gaining 25 kg over 2 years. Her BMI is now 36 kg/m² and her neck circumference has increased. She has no anatomical abnormality of the jaw or tonsils. Her symptoms improved previously when she lost weight.
questions.q: Which mechanism best explains how her weight gain caused her condition?
o: Fat deposition narrowing the pharyngeal airway
questions.e: Excess pharyngeal fat in obesity narrows the airway so it collapses more easily during sleep.

steps.x: The question asks: Which mechanism best explains how her weight gain caused her condition?
Weight gain with a larger neck.

elim: Not the mechanism; effort is preserved in OSA.
Not a feature of OSA.
Relates to central or hypoventilation syndromes.
Asthma mechanism, not upper airway collapse.

steps.x: B: Fat deposition narrowing the pharyngeal airway. Obesity worsens OSA through excess pharyngeal fat.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man with obstructive sleep apnoea sleeps 8 hours a night but wakes unrefreshed and falls asleep at his desk. He has no memory of waking during the night. Polysomnography shows 40 events per hour, each ending in a brief arousal. His awake PaCO2 is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his daytime sleepiness?
questions.e: Each apnoea ends in an arousal; repeated arousals fragment sleep architecture, so sleep is unrefreshing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for his daytime sleepiness?

clues: each ending in a brief arousal
steps.x: Enough hours, but interrupted by arousals.

elim: His awake PaCO2 is normal.
Nothing suggests it.
He sleeps 8 hours.
The key mechanism is repeated arousal fragmenting sleep.

steps.x: B: Fragmented sleep from repeated arousals. Sleepiness in OSA comes from fragmented sleep, not short sleep.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man with obstructive sleep apnoea has overnight polysomnography. During each event airflow stops, oxygen saturation falls to around 84% and then, after about 30 seconds, he gasps and breathing restarts. His BMI is 34 kg/m². He asks what makes his breathing start again.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism that ends each apnoea?
o: Arousal triggered by hypoxia and hypercapnia
questions.e: Rising CO2 and falling O2 trigger an arousal that restores pharyngeal muscle tone and airway patency.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism that ends each apnoea?
Desaturation then gasp.

elim: Not the trigger for restarting breathing.
A cause of collapse, not what ends it.
Lower airway; irrelevant to pharyngeal collapse.
A slow chronic effect over weeks.

steps.x: A: Arousal triggered by hypoxia and hypercapnia. Hypoxia/hypercapnia trigger arousal to reopen the airway.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has hypertension that has been hard to control. He has loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas, and polysomnography confirms severe obstructive sleep apnoea. Renal function, aldosterone/renin ratio and renal artery imaging are normal. His BP is 162/98 mmHg. After 3 months of CPAP his BP falls to 138/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypertension?
questions.e: Recurrent nocturnal hypoxia activates the sympathetic nervous system, raising systemic blood pressure; treating OSA lowers it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypertension?

clues: aldosterone/renin ratio and renal artery imaging are normal
steps.x: Secondary causes excluded and BP improves with CPAP.

elim: EPO causes polycythaemia, not the main driver of hypertension.
Aldosterone/renin ratio is normal.
Renal artery imaging is normal.
Renal function is normal.

steps.x: E: Sympathetic activation from recurrent hypoxia. OSA hypertension = sympathetic activation from recurrent hypoxia.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman starts CPAP for moderate obstructive sleep apnoea. After 2 weeks her husband says the snoring and pauses have stopped and she feels more alert. Her BMI is unchanged at 35 kg/m². She asks how the machine works, since it only blows room air through a mask.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of her treatment?
o: Splints the upper airway open with positive pressure
questions.e: CPAP keeps a positive airway pressure throughout the respiratory cycle, splinting the pharynx open.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of her treatment?
Benefit without weight change or oxygen.

elim: CPAP blows room air, not oxygen.
Drive is not the problem in OSA.
Her weight is unchanged.
A bronchodilator mechanism, not relevant here.

steps.x: E: Splints the upper airway open with positive pressure. CPAP is a pneumatic splint for the pharynx.
